Lessons.Title: Tessellations of the Plane
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: characterize a tessellation as a gapless, overlap-free cover of a region by repeated shapes, and justify how translations, rotations or reflections position tiles.
A rectangular grid tessellates because copies meet at whole edges and four right angles meet at each interior vertex. Merely placing many identical shapes close together does not guarantee no gaps.

Draw an original irregular quadrilateral on squared paper, make rotated and translated copies, and test edge-to-edge fit. A teacher evaluates whether the actual drawing covers the selected region without gaps or overlaps, not just arithmetic.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tessellation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Tiling of the plane without gaps or overlaps.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Tiles must cover each region point consistently.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertex angle sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: Angles of tiles around an interior point total 360°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rigid-copy tile
KeyConcepts.Definition: Tile retains original side lengths and angles when moved.

WorkedExamples.Title: Square corners
WorkedExamples.Question: How many 90° square corners fill a vertex?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide a full turn by each corner.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four copies leave no angular gap.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangle corners
WorkedExamples.Question: How many 60° equilateral triangle corners fill a point?
Steps: Six sectors meet without angular gap.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject gap
WorkedExamples.Question: Three square corners meet at a vertex. What angle is unfilled?
WorkedExamples.Check: Three squares alone cannot fill the point.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming equal tile areas alone imply tessellation.
Counting tile overlap as extra coverage.

SummaryPoints: Tessellations have no gaps or overlaps.
Analyze vertex angles and edge matching.

Visuals.Title: Fill 360 degrees around a vertex
Visuals.Description: Each indicated regular tile shape can meet without gaps when vertex angles sum to 360°.

Lessons.Title: Regular Tessellations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: investigate which congruent regular polygons alone make an edge-to-edge regular tessellation, using interior-angle reasoning.
A regular n-gon has interior angle ((n−2)×180°)/n. Equilateral triangles (60°), squares (90°) and regular hexagons (120°) fit integer numbers around a point; regular pentagons (108°) do not.
Construct original samples from paper or a grid. Test hexagonal honeycomb and explain why three 120° corners close. Teacher review assesses regularity, edge matching and explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Regular polygon
KeyConcepts.Definition: All sides and all interior angles equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertex divisibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: Number of corners around point must be a whole number.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 360°/interior angle must be integer for regular single-polygon tiling.

KeyConcepts.Title: Excluded pentagon
KeyConcepts.Example: Cannot make a regular pentagon-only edge-to-edge tessellation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Hexagon tiling
WorkedExamples.Question: How many 120° regular-hexagon corners meet at a point?

WorkedExamples.Title: Pentagon obstacle
WorkedExamples.Question: Can 108° pentagons fill a point with only identical corners?
WorkedExamples.Check: Regular pentagons alone cannot form a regular tessellation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangle regular tiling
WorkedExamples.Question: How many equilateral triangles around a vertex?
WorkedExamples.Check: They can form a regular triangular tiling.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using exterior angle instead of interior.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Tiles meet by their interior corners.

SummaryPoints: Regular triangle, square and hexagon tilings are possible.

Visuals.Title: Hexagonal corners around a point
Visuals.Description: Exactly three hexagon angles of 120° sum to 360°.

Lessons.Title: Tessellating Polygons
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: design a tessellation with polygons that may be different or irregular, showing explicitly how tile edges meet and whether a repeat pattern covers the plane.

Every triangle tessellates the plane by pairing rotated copies into parallelograms, and every quadrilateral can tile by 180° rotations around side midpoints in an appropriate arrangement. Not every arbitrary mixture will tile.

Make an original triangle tile with unequal sides and demonstrate a paired copy. Ask a partner to explain how translated parallelograms extend the pattern. Teacher review assesses the actual edge-matching diagram and reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle tiling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two copies of a triangle can form a parallelogram.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Rotate one triangle 180° about a side midpoint.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallelogram tiling
KeyConcepts.Rule: Translate repeated copies along two edge vectors.
KeyConcepts.Example: A nonrectangular parallelogram covers plane in rows.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed polygon tiling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiple polygon shapes can meet if vertex angles and edges fit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Triangles and hexagons can form patterns in some configurations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangle corner sum
WorkedExamples.Question: Two triangles each contribute angle sum 180°. What total angles?
Steps: A suitable arrangement can close a full angular turn.
WorkedExamples.Check: Actual edge placement must still be checked.

WorkedExamples.Title: Parallelogram area
WorkedExamples.Question: A tiling tile has base 5 and perpendicular height 3. What area?

WorkedExamples.Title: Area of tiled patch
WorkedExamples.Question: Twelve nonoverlapping 15-unit² tiles fill a patch. What area?
WorkedExamples.Check: No gaps assumed for exact patch coverage.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming angle sum alone proves edge fit.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Edges may mismatch even when corner totals align.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a distorted copy instead of a rigid tile.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A tessellation by congruent copies preserves dimensions.

SummaryPoints: Tile arrangements must match at edges and vertices.
Verify periodic coverage with a repeat cell.

Lessons.Title: What Influences Temperature?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: identify candidate predictors for temperature data, distinguish measurements from explanatory claims and examine how geographical and seasonal variables could confound a model.

Latitude, elevation, distance from ocean, season and time of day may influence observed temperature. A bivariate graph of latitude and temperature may show an association, but a single predictor cannot account for all geographic variation.

Use independent fictional city observations (latitude 20°, temperature 30°C),(40°,20°C),(60°,10°C). Predict a trend, then discuss limitations such as elevation. A teacher assesses model assumptions and causal reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Predictor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Input used to estimate an output variable.

KeyConcepts.Title: Confounding variable
KeyConcepts.Definition: Another factor influencing the observed relation.
KeyConcepts.Example: Mountain cities may be cooler at same latitude.

KeyConcepts.Title: Association versus causation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A trend does not isolate its physical cause.
KeyConcepts.Example: Higher latitude often accompanies lower temperature in some seasonal samples.

WorkedExamples.Title: Temperature trend
WorkedExamples.Question: Fictional pairs (20,30),(40,20),(60,10) have what slope?
WorkedExamples.Check: The fictional samples lie on a decreasing line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict mid-latitude
WorkedExamples.Question: Use model T=40−0.5L for L=50°.
WorkedExamples.Check: Model is illustrative, not a weather forecast.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find contextual intercept
WorkedExamples.Question: For T=40−0.5L, predicted T at zero latitude?
WorkedExamples.Check: Not a measured universal equator temperature.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a simplified sample as real global climate data.
Using different months to compare locations without noting season.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align or account for observation times.

SummaryPoints: Models depend on predictor and context.

Lessons.Title: Plotting the Weather
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: construct a scatter plot from paired climate-like measurements and choose a reasonable linear model with a stated numerical slope, intercept and uncertainty.

Given original fictional observations of latitude L and temperature T: (20,31),(30,24),(40,21),(50,14), one possible trend line is T≈40−0.5L. Some observations fall above or below the line; its predictions are estimates.
Draw the points and fitted line with labeled units. Compare residuals at each observation and explain why the line is not a universal physical law. A teacher reviews graph quality and justification.

KeyConcepts.Title: Weather scatter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Paired measurements with geographic x and temperature y.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Each point is one paired observation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fitted model
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line summarizing data rather than exactly passing through every dot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Residual
KeyConcepts.Example: At L=20, prediction 30 and observation 31 gives +1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Residual above line
WorkedExamples.Question: At L=20, measured T=31 and model predicts 30. Residual?
WorkedExamples.Check: Observation is one degree above model.

WorkedExamples.Title: Residual below line
WorkedExamples.Question: At L=50, measured 14 and predicted 15. Residual?
WorkedExamples.Check: The dot lies below the model line.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Connecting points as chronological weather series.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: City latitudes are independent subjects rather than one timeline.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use scatter plot and fitted line.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Pretending model predictions are exact observations.

SummaryPoints: Scatter plots preserve paired weather observations.

Lessons.Title: Using and Interpreting a Mathematical Model
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use a linear model of paired data for contextual predictions, interpret slope and intercept, and explicitly state plausible limits and uncertainty.

An illustrative model T(L)=40−0.5L for temperature T in degrees Celsius versus latitude L in degrees has negative slope, but its intercept describes only what the model predicts for L=0. It is not an asserted universal equatorial measurement, nor necessarily suitable for southern latitudes, other seasons, or extreme altitudes.

Student task: use a fictional fitted model to predict temperatures at two unmeasured latitudes and defend whether the model can support the inference. A teacher checks argumentation, context, extrapolation, units and the model’s limitations, not just numeric predictions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model prediction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Evaluate fitted rule at new x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Slope interpretation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Estimated change in output for one unit increase of input.
KeyConcepts.Example: Increasing L by 10 predicts a 5°C decrease.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intercept limitation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Predicted output when input zero, not necessarily an observed value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict one city
WorkedExamples.Question: Model T=40−0.5L predicts what at L=45°?
WorkedExamples.Check: Not an observed or live weather forecast.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret slope
WorkedExamples.Question: What does slope −0.5 mean for an increase of 10 latitude degrees?
WorkedExamples.Check: A fitted trend is not a causal statement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Limit extrapolation
WorkedExamples.Question: Model fitted only for L=20° to 50°. Is predicting L=90° an interpolation?
Steps: Observed latitudes in fictional data are 20°–50°.
Using model there is extrapolation with potentially large error.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; it is extrapolation and should be treated cautiously.
WorkedExamples.Check: Other weather and geographic factors matter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling the intercept a physically verified temperature at latitude zero.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A fitted model’s intercept may lie outside measured data.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State it is a model prediction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming causal effect of latitude from a scatter plot alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Confounding variables may explain part of association.

SummaryPoints: Interpret slope with units and relevant domain.
State limits of extrapolation and alternative factors.
